refocus-present-stop-mind-wandering.reason: Replace inherited generic mind-wandering and treatment-like claims with a narrow auditory attention-flexibility drill that matches core Attention Training Technique operations described in systematic-review literature: externally focused selective attention, deliberate switching, and divided attention. Preserve uncertainty about clinical effects and do not present the simplified drill as Metacognitive Therapy or a treatment.
refocus-present-stop-mind-wandering.title: Deliberate Attention Switching with Everyday Sounds
refocus-present-stop-mind-wandering.subtitle: Practice selecting, switching, and broadening external attention
refocus-present-stop-mind-wandering.description: Use several neutral sounds around you to practice deliberately selecting one sound, switching to another, and then noticing several at once. Treat this as an attention-flexibility drill, not a treatment for worry, anxiety, or another condition.

lifeOsSource.hack: Practice deliberately moving external attention among several neutral sounds.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Find a safe place with several ordinary sounds. Attend closely to one sound without needing to block the others. Deliberately switch to a second and then a third sound. Finish by broadening attention so several sounds can be noticed together. Keep the exercise brief and stop when you choose.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Could you intentionally select, switch, and broaden attention? Record the skill you practiced, not whether worry or another symptom changed.
lifeOsSource.reference: Attention Training Technique is an auditory metacognitive intervention using externally focused selective attention, attention switching, and divided attention. Recent systematic-review evidence describes possible attentional effects but variable study quality, while a randomized study in probable generalized anxiety disorder did not find ATT superior to its control condition on worry outcomes.

faq.question: Is this the standard Attention Training Technique or Metacognitive Therapy?
faq.answer: No. It is a simplified educational drill based on the attention operations described in ATT research. Formal ATT has a defined protocol, and Metacognitive Therapy is a broader treatment.

faq.question: Will this reduce worry or anxiety?
faq.answer: Brali does not make that promise. Research on ATT is mixed across outcomes and study designs; one randomized study in people with probable generalized anxiety disorder found no advantage over the control condition for worry measures.

faq.question: What should I measure?
faq.answer: Measure the controllable skill: whether you could deliberately select one sound, switch attention when intended, and broaden attention afterward. Do not treat a short-term symptom change as proof of treatment effect.

intro.html: Attention Training Technique research describes deliberate practice in externally focused selective attention, switching attention, and dividing or broadening attention. Brali extracts those observable attention operations into a small educational drill while keeping the clinical claims outside the protocol.

sections.title: 1. Choose several neutral sounds
sections.html: Use ordinary sounds in a safe environment: ventilation, distant traffic, birds, footsteps, a clock, or other neutral background sounds. You do not need special audio or headphones.

sections.title: 2. Select one sound
sections.html: Direct attention toward one sound and notice its changes. The goal is not to erase other sounds but to practice choosing the current target.

sections.title: 3. Switch deliberately
sections.html: Choose a different sound and move attention to it on purpose. Repeat with another sound. Notice the act of switching rather than judging whether concentration feels perfect.

sections.title: 4. Broaden attention
sections.html: Finish by allowing several sounds into awareness together. This changes the task from selecting one target to holding a wider external field.

sections.title: Evidence boundary
sections.html: ATT has been studied as a metacognitive intervention, but evidence varies by sample, outcome, protocol fidelity, and study quality. A recent systematic review found a mixed-quality evidence base, and a randomized study of probable generalized anxiety disorder did not find ATT superior to control for worry outcomes. This simplified Brali drill therefore claims only to practice attention selection and switching.
